faqs.question: What should I be for Halloween if I can't decide?
faqs.answer: Answer six questions in order: budget, free hours, who you are going with, comfort, weather and scare level. Each one removes options, so you end with two or three that fit, and the research on choice overload suggests a short list leaves you happier with the pick.

faqs.question: How many costume ideas should I shortlist?
faqs.answer: Three is plenty. In Peterson and Cheng's 2020 study, choosing from 16 options was linked to more decision difficulty than choosing from 4, so a longer list mostly adds doubt.

faqs.question: When should I decide on my Halloween costume?
faqs.answer: Shortlist by 24 October and decide by 27 October, which leaves four days to gather pieces. In 2026 that is a Saturday and a Tuesday before Halloween on Saturday 31 October; in 2027 it is a Sunday and a Wednesday before Sunday 31 October.

faqs.question: What can I go as for Halloween with almost no money?
faqs.answer: Build from your wardrobe plus one prop, such as a torch, a headset or a peaked cap. An usher at a ghost-only screening needs dark clothes, a torch and a tray of sweets, so it stays under an estimated $10 or ₹800 if you own the clothes.

faqs.question: What should I be for Halloween if it's cold outside?
faqs.answer: Choose a costume that goes over your coat or is the coat, such as a night porter at a haunted railway station in your own coat and a peaked cap. If the forecast three days out shows below about 10°C, skip anything that only works bare-armed.

faqs.question: What should my partner and I be for Halloween?
faqs.answer: Pick a pair where each half looks unfinished alone, like a bat and the sound recordist chasing it, or a ghost and the neighbour filing a noise complaint. Agree on it early, because two people deciding takes longer than one.

faqs.question: How do we choose a group costume without endless arguing?
faqs.answer: Vote on the theme only, then let each person pick a role inside it. A haunted choir or a waxwork museum on its night shift works for 3 to 6 people, and everyone mostly wears their own clothes.

faqs.question: Should my costume be scary or cute?
faqs.answer: Rate the night from 0 (cute) to 3 (gore) and cap it at 1 if children under about 8 will be there. Save creepy makeup for an adult party and a weekend with time for a practice run.

faqs.question: Why do I keep changing my mind about my costume?
faqs.answer: You may be maximizing, hunting for the single best option. Schwartz and colleagues found maximizers report more regret and less satisfaction with purchases than people who stop at good enough, so set a deadline and accept a strong second choice.

faqs.question: What should I be for Halloween if I hate dressing up?
faqs.answer: Wear your normal clothes and add one prop you can remove in five seconds, like a headset and a name badge that turns you into a ghost in customer service. It shows you joined in without hours in an itchy outfit.

article.contentMarkdown:
# What to Be for Halloween: Answer Six Questions, Get Your Costume

What to be for Halloween comes down to six questions, asked in order: how much you will spend, how many hours you have, who you are going with, how comfortable you need to be, what the weather will do, and how scary you want to look. Answer them and the costume internet shrinks to two or three options that fit your night.

Decide early, because most people don't. The nearest festival data SubhSandesh holds is Raksha Bandhan 2026, where 49.4% of 89 pages were built on the day itself and 27.0% the day before; that is another festival entirely and n = 89 is small, so read it as a hint about timing only. Plan the photo too: 48.3% of the pages we host get opened on a phone, so shoot vertical. Below are the flowchart, where each path ends, and a deadline that stops the scrolling.

## Why is choosing a Halloween costume so hard?

Choosing a costume is a textbook case of choice overload: the more options in front of you, the harder the decision feels and the less you enjoy the pick. In [Iyengar and Lepper's 2000 experiments](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/11138768), people were more likely to buy jam or chocolate when offered 6 kinds than 24 or 30, and were more satisfied with what they chose from the short list.

A later test points the same way. Peterson and Cheng gave 228 adults either 4 or 16 options, and [the 16-option condition went with greater decision difficulty](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC7487285) in both a shopping task and a gamble task.

[Schwartz and colleagues (2002)](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/12416921) found that maximizers, who hunt for the single best option, report more regret and less satisfaction with purchases than satisficers, who stop at good enough. The flowchart below is built to make you a satisficer well before 31 October.

## The six-question costume flowchart

Budget and time are hard limits, so they come first; scare level is taste, so it comes last. By question 6 you should land on one of the five endpoints in the next section.

### 1. What is your budget?

Money narrows the field faster than taste. Every figure here is a rough estimate, not a quote.

- **Under about $10 or ₹800:** your wardrobe plus one prop. Endpoint A.
- **About $10 to $40, or ₹800 to ₹3,000:** buy one hero piece, such as a wig, hat or cape, and pull the rest from home. Every endpoint stays open.
- **Above that:** only if you will wear it again.

### 2. How much time do you have before 31 October?

Halloween falls on Saturday 31 October 2026 and Sunday 31 October 2027. Count free hours, not days.

- **Under 2 hours:** endpoint A.
- **One free evening:** endpoints A, B or C.
- **A weekend or more:** endpoint E opens up, since scare makeup needs a practice run.

### 3. Are you going solo, as a pair or in a group?

Company turns choosing into agreeing. Agreeing always takes longer.

- **Solo:** any endpoint, decided alone.
- **A pair:** endpoint C.
- **A group of 3 to 6:** endpoint D. Vote on the theme only, then each picks a role.

### 4. How comfortable do you need to be?

Think of your longest stretch in costume. A 4-hour party and a 2-hour trick-or-treat walk need different things.

- **More than 3 hours on your feet:** your own shoes, nothing itchy on your face, no mask that narrows what you see at the edges.
- **Seated most of the night:** skip tails, wings and anything rigid at the hips.
- **You dislike dressing up:** endpoint A, one prop you can remove in 5 seconds.

### 5. What will the weather be on the night?

Check the forecast about 3 days out. Dress for the walk between doors, not the warm room.

- **Below about 10°C:** the costume goes over a coat, or is the coat. Endpoint B.
- **Rain likely:** no paper, card or felt; choose something that works with a hood up.
- **Above about 25°C:** thin layers, no fur, no full-head pieces, and carry water.

### 6. How scary do you want to be?

Rate your night from 0 to 3: 0 is cute, 1 is eerie, 2 is creepy, 3 is gore. If children under about 8 will be present, cap yourself at 1.

- **0 or 1:** any endpoint, played gently.
- **2:** endpoint E with pale makeup and no blood.
- **3:** endpoint E plus fake wounds, with a skin patch-test of the products days before.

## Where each path ends: five endpoints and 9 original costumes

The table groups the endpoints by the answers that lead to them; costs and times are estimates for a costume built mostly from what you own.

| Endpoint | Answers that lead here | Estimated cost | Estimated prep |
|---|---|---|---|
| A. Closet plus one prop | Low budget, under 2 hours, or you dislike costumes | Under $10 / ₹800 | 15–60 minutes |
| B. Layer over your coat | Cold or wet night, long time outdoors | $10–25 / ₹800–2,000 | 1–2 hours |
| C. Two-part pair | A couple or two friends | $10–40 / ₹800–3,000 for both | 2–3 hours |
| D. Group theme with roles | 3 to 6 people, one shared idea | $5–15 / ₹400–1,200 each | 1 hour each |
| E. Full scare build | Scare level 2–3, a weekend free | $20–40 / ₹1,500–3,000 | 4–6 hours with a practice run |

A is the cheapest and B the warmest, which makes them the safest defaults. The ideas below were written for this guide, two or so per endpoint:

- **A. Usher at a ghost-only screening:** dark clothes, a torch with red tape over the lens, and a tray of sweets you offer to empty chairs.
- **A. A ghost in customer service:** a headset, pale makeup and a name badge reading "Here to help since 1889".
- **B. Night porter at a haunted railway station:** your own coat, a peaked cap, a torch and a hand-lettered "Last train: 1897" sign.
- **C. A bat and the sound recordist chasing it:** one in black with fabric wings, the other in headphones holding a broom-handle boom mic with a fluffy sock on the end.
- **C. A ghost and the neighbour filing a noise complaint:** one in pale makeup rattling a bunch of old keys, the other in pyjamas with a clipboard of grievances.
- **D. A haunted choir:** matching dark tops, pale faces, battery candles, and one empty music stand carried everywhere for the conductor who never came back.
- **D. Night shift at a waxwork museum:** each person freezes as a figure from a different century, while one visitor keeps checking whether anyone moved.
- **E. Victorian ghost photographer:** black cloth over head and shoulders, a box-style camera, sunken-eye makeup, guests "captured" one by one.
- **E. Taxidermist after closing time:** a leather apron, glass-eye earrings and a stuffed toy fox you speak to softly.

## Borrow a trait: let the costume do some of the work

A costume can be a role that changes how you act for the night. In [a 2017 *Child Development* study by White and colleagues](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/27982409), 180 children aged 4 and 6 did a dull task for 10 minutes beside an attractive video game. Those who pretended to be a character such as Batman kept working longest, ahead of children using the third person and, last, those saying "I".

It was young children in a lab, and only the abstract was read for this guide, so do not stretch it to adults. It still makes a fair tiebreaker between two finalists: hosting for 4 hours suits the endlessly patient customer-service ghost, and a night where you know nobody suits the usher, whose whole job is greeting people.

## Set a decision deadline, not a longer list

Late deciding is normal: not one of the 89 Raksha Bandhan 2026 pages on SubhSandesh was built more than 7 days ahead. Different festival, small n, familiar habit.

So give the decision a date. For 2026, shortlist 3 costumes by Saturday 24 October and decide by Tuesday 27 October; in 2027 those dates fall on Sunday and Wednesday. Three is well under the 16 options that made choosing harder for Peterson and Cheng's participants.

Still tied on the 27th? Take the finalist that needs fewer purchases, since it is the one most likely to be finished.

## Send the costume reveal to the one person who should see it

Someone absent on the night may still want to see it. Our [interactive Halloween card, which holds six photos,](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) is roughly a 5-minute build: the recipient knocks at a little haunted house, carves a lantern until its candle catches, then polishes steamed-up portraits until your pictures appear. Its closing Boo License has you choose what *they* should be, from eight options running from ghost to bat.

For a bigger reveal, the [premium Halloween page with a 60-second voice note](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) needs around 10 minutes, fits 12 photos for a before-and-after run, can stay locked until a time you set, and lets them send one reply. Of everyone building on SubhSandesh, 38.5% add a password before sharing. And if you landed on endpoint C but still need a partner, a [date invitation page](https://subhsandesh.in/date-invitation) asks first.

## When this flowchart, or our page, is the wrong tool

Skip the flowchart if you already love an idea: these six questions break ties, they should not talk you out of a costume that makes you grin. Skip it when a party sets a theme, or when a child picks their own costume.

We have limits as well. Each page greets one person, every screen is in English, and none of them will invite a crowd, sell you a wig or match you with a costume partner. If the person you want to impress is standing beside you on the night, skip the link and do a twirl.

## Sources

- S. S. Iyengar and M. R. Lepper, [When choice is demotivating](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/11138768), *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* 79(6), December 2000. Abstract read.
- B. Schwartz et al., [Maximizing versus satisficing: happiness is a matter of choice](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/12416921), *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* 83(5), November 2002. Abstract read.
- N. Peterson and J. Cheng, [Decision experience in hyperchoice: the role of numeracy and age differences](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC7487285), *Current Psychology*, online 14 September 2020. Full text read.
- R. E. White et al., [The "Batman Effect": improving perseverance in young children](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/27982409), *Child Development* 88(5), 2017, online 16 December 2016. Abstract read.

sources.stat: Across 3 field and lab experiments, people were more likely to buy gourmet jams or chocolates (or write optional essays) when offered 6 options rather than 24 or 30, and reported greater satisfaction with selections from the limited set. Abstract only read (JPSP, not open access).

Maximization correlated negatively with happiness, optimism, self-esteem and life satisfaction and positively with regret; maximizers were less satisfied than satisficers with consumer decisions. Abstract only read (JPSP, not open access).

116 older and 112 younger adults (228) chose from 16 options (hyperchoice) or 4 options; hyperchoice was related to greater decision difficulty in both the consumer and the gamble task. Full text read (open access).

180 children aged 4 and 6 did a repetitive task for 10 minutes with an attractive video game available; those who impersonated an exemplar such as Batman spent the most time working, then third-person self-talk, then first person. Abstract only read (Child Development, not open access).

serpOverlap.method: One WebSearch call (US index), 2026-10-13, 9 results; all 9 are weak (hijacked-subdomain spam x5, a 2019 school paper, a telecom company blog, a 2009 Q&A scrape, a forum archive). None appears in the sibling research briefs or serps.md.

structuralLimitations: No Halloween or costume first-party data exists in facts.md; first-party lines are the Raksha Bandhan lead-time analogue (disclosed in body as a different festival, n = 89) and platform-wide phone share and password rate.

SERP: 1 WebSearch (US index), 9 results, all weak. Every fetchable page returned 403/521 or failed (bvtigernews 403, airtalkwireless 403 Cloudflare block, hteknologi 521, ntwcontabilidade and intrafocus fetch failed), so the SERP was judged from titles and snippets only.

Three of four sources were read as abstracts only (JPSP x2, Child Development); Peterson & Cheng 2020 was read in full. White et al. 2017 is a child lab study; the body says so and does not extend it to adults.
Cost and prep figures in the table are labelled estimates, not measured prices.
Weather thresholds (10°C, 25°C) and the scare cap for children under about 8 are editorial rules of thumb, not sourced figures; the body labels them as 'about'.
